title: Self-Consistency Boosts Calibration for Math Reasoning
authors: Ante Wang, Linfeng Song, Ye Tian, Baolin Peng, Lifeng Jin, Haitao Mi, Jinsong Su, Dong Yu
text:
Mathematical reasoning tasks [1,2,3] involve mapping a question into a series of equations, which are then solved to obtain the final answer. Math reasoning has long been recognized challenging. Existing solutions propose to map input questions into equations via semantic parsing [4,5] or AST decoding [6,7,8]. Yet, the performance can degradate dramatically even with slight changes to the questions [9,10].

Recently, large language models (LLM, [11,12,13]) have shown great potential for solving many math reasoning tasks, even though they are not specifically trained on these tasks. For instance, with chain-of-thought prompting [14] and self-consistency [15], open-source LLMs, such as Mixtral 8 \times 7B [13], can reach an accuracy of around 80% on the GSM8K benchmark [1]. On the other hand, conventional pretrained models (e.g., T5 [16]) that are specifically finetuned on the GSM8K training set can only report accuracies around 10% to 20% [17,18].

However, LLMs lack adequate calibration out of the box – the probabilities of model predictions are often poorly aligned with the actual accuracy [19,20]. Calibration is important for LLM development, as a well-calibrated LLM can precisely tell how likely its responses are correct or not. With such information, LLM developers can take multiple options to handle low-confidence responses, such as letting the LLM refuse to answer or keep resampling until a confident response is produced.

In this work, we propose calibration methods based on self-consistency [15] for math reasoning tasks. Self-consistency performs clustering over multiple LLM samples before picking one from the largest cluster as the response to each input query. Here we consider several ways to estimate model confidence using the clustering results: cluster size that estimates how many samples agree with the selected one, cluster number that measures to what extent samples disagree with each other, and pairwise comparison that captures relative differences between pairs of clusters.

We conduct experiments using strong open-source LLMs: Mistral [21,13] and LLaMA2 [12] series models with / without being aligned with instructions. Results on GSM8K [1] and MathQA [3] show that all our methods better calibrate these models than exiting popular methods, such as p(True) [22] and logit [23] over the whole reasoning path or target answer span only.
